added_not_in_notes: Chapter 26 and 27 openings ('Where we are' introductions), 'Try it' questions with answers, and 'Remember' summaries; none are in the notes.

Arabic equivalents for key terms not given in the notes: الترجمة السمعية البصرية (AVT), التعليق الصوتي (voice-over, replacing the notes' المعلق), الوصف الصوتي (audio description), نظرية الغاية (Skopos theory), السترجة / الترجمة المرئية (subtitling), قائمة الحوار (dialogue list), مصطلح ذو خصوصية ثقافية (culture-bound term), اللغة المحظورة (taboo language), الرقابة (censorship). Only الدبلجة (dubbing) comes from the notes.
Dubbing in the Arab world: used for many children's programmes and series (Chapter 26, Step 2), replacing the notes' 'Europe, America and Asia'.

A real dubbing example: The Simpsons dubbed into Arabic as آل شمشون, with Homer's beer changed to a soft drink (Chapter 26, Step 2), cited to (Translation Team, n.d.). It is not in either AVT notes document.
A Skopos example: a cartoon for children versus a documentary for adults (Chapter 26, Step 3).

Chapter 26, Step 5 'take your first steps': watch the whole video, then read the script; ask for the brief (subtitles or dubbing, which viewers, which Arabic); practise with free software (Subtitle Edit, Aegisub); watch Arabic-subtitled films and notice what was shortened.

Cross-references to earlier chapters: Chapter 3 (English–Arabic differences), Chapters 14 to 16 (cultural references), Chapter 14 (culture-specific item), Chapters 12 and 13 (procedures and strategies); and in Chapter 1 and 'Start here' (c2a.js), pointers to Part 9.
Subtitle timing: display time of about one to six or seven seconds, and the term 'spotting' for marking in and out times (Chapter 27, Step 1; Díaz Cintas & Remael, 2021).
The corrected line-length standard: about 37 to 39 characters per line, up to 42 on streaming platforms, and 'always follow the client’s guidelines' (Chapter 27, Step 1).

SDH (subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing), which also describe sounds, and subtitles for language learners, as examples of intralingual subtitles; 'interlingual: what translators usually make' (Chapter 27, Step 1). SDH also added to the Abbreviations list.
Subtitling definition extended to on-screen text and song lyrics (Chapter 27 key term).
A five-step subtitling method: watch, spot, translate, condense, check (Chapter 27, Step 2).
A worked condensing example: 'Well, you know, I really don’t think we should go out tonight, because it’s going to rain.' → لا أظنّ أن علينا الخروج الليلة، فالمطر قادم. (Chapter 27, Step 2).

Rules for Arabic subtitles: write in MSA even for dialect speakers unless the client asks otherwise; break lines at meaning boundaries (noun with adjective, preposition with noun, pairs such as مدير المدرسة); use Arabic punctuation (Chapter 27, Step 3).
Advice to keep sociolect, slang and idiolect 'even in MSA ... through your choice of words' (Chapter 27, Step 3).
Conditions on two strategies: official equivalent 'if there is one'; omission 'when it is unimportant and there is no space' (Chapter 27, Step 4).

Two further reasons for softening taboo language: swear words look stronger in writing than in speech, and audiences have different norms; plus 'keep the emotion of the scene where you can' (Chapter 27, Step 5).
A definition of censorship: 'Removing or changing content that is considered unacceptable' (Chapter 27 key term).
